title: Soil: The Living Ground
summary: What soil is made of, how it forms from rock over a very long time, the living things that keep it healthy, its layers and types, and why people must protect it.
poll: Soil is just dirt, so it is not worth protecting.

versions.title: The Living Ground
versions.text:
Pick up a scoop of soil. It looks like dirt. But soil is full of life!

Soil has bits of rock. It has bits of dead plants too. They rot. They get dark and soft. This dark part is humus. Soil holds air and water too.

Soil comes from rock. Sun, rain, and ice break rock. Roots crack it. Bit by bit, the rock gets small. This takes a long time. It can take a thousand years to make a thin layer.

Lots of things live in soil. A handful has more life than there are people on Earth! Most is too small to see.

An earthworm digs in the soil. It digs paths. Air and water go down them. Bugs eat dead leaves. Germs help too. This makes food for plants.

Soil has a top layer. It is dark and rich. Most roots grow there. Next comes a light one. At the base is rock.

Most of our food grows in soil. But wind and rain can take soil away. This is called erosion. Roots hold soil in place. So Saudi Arabia will plant trees. It will plant lots!

Soil is made from rock. Sun, rain, wind, and ice break rock into small bits. Plant roots crack it too. This takes a long time. It can take a thousand years to make just one thin layer of soil.

Lots of living things are in soil. A handful has more of them than there are people on Earth! Most are too small to see.

An earthworm digs tunnels in the soil. Air and water go down the tunnels to plant roots. Small bugs eat dead leaves. Tiny germs break the leaves down. This turns them into food for plants.

Soil has layers. The top layer is dark and rich. Most roots grow there. Below it is a pale layer with less humus. At the very bottom is hard rock.

Most of our food grows in soil. But wind and rain can carry soil away. This is called erosion. Plant roots hold soil in place. That is one reason Saudi Arabia plans to plant ten billion trees.

versions.title: Soil: The Living Ground
versions.text:
When you pick up a scoop of soil, it may look like plain dirt. In fact, soil is one of the most important materials on Earth, because almost all of our food depends on it.

Soil is a mixture. About half of it is minerals, which are tiny bits of broken rock. A small part is humus, the dark, soft material that forms when dead plants and animals rot. The rest is air and water, which fill the spaces between the pieces.

Soil forms from rock. Over many years, heat, cold, rain, wind, and ice break rock into smaller and smaller pieces. Plant roots grow into cracks and split the rock apart. This process is extremely slow. It can take as long as a thousand years to form a single centimeter of soil.

Healthy soil is full of life. A handful can hold more living things than there are people on Earth, though most are too small to see. Earthworms dig tunnels that let air and water reach plant roots. Bacteria and fungi decompose, or break down, dead leaves. As they do, they release nutrients that plants need to grow.

Soil has layers. The topsoil is dark and rich in humus, and most roots grow there. Below it lies the subsoil, which is paler and contains less humus. Deeper still is solid rock.

Wind and rain can carry soil away, especially when no plants cover the ground. This loss is called erosion. Farmers protect soil by planting crops that cover the ground and by adding compost, a mixture of rotted food scraps and leaves. In Saudi Arabia, where many soils are sandy, plans to plant ten billion trees will also help hold the ground in place.

versions.title: Soil: The Living Ground
versions.text:
When you pick up a scoop of soil, it may look like ordinary dirt, yet soil is one of the most valuable materials on Earth, because almost all of the food that people eat depends on it in some way.

Soil is a mixture of several ingredients. Approximately half of it consists of minerals, which are tiny fragments of broken rock, while a small portion is humus, the dark, soft material that forms when dead plants and animals decay, and the remainder is air and water, which fill the spaces between the particles.

Soil forms from rock through a process called weathering, in which heat, cold, rain, wind, and ice break rock into progressively smaller fragments over many years, while plant roots push into cracks and gradually split the rock apart. Because this process is extremely slow, it can take as long as a thousand years to form a single centimeter of soil.

Healthy soil is full of life, since a handful can contain more living organisms than there are people on Earth, although most of them are microscopic. Earthworms dig tunnels that allow air and water to reach plant roots, and their waste adds richness to the ground. Meanwhile, decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead leaves, and in the process they release nutrients that plants need to grow.

Soil is arranged in layers. The topsoil is dark and rich in humus, and it is where most roots grow, while beneath it lies the subsoil, which is paler and contains less humus, and deeper still is solid rock.

Soils also differ in texture. Sandy soil has large grains, so water drains through it quickly, whereas clay soil has extremely small particles that hold water and become sticky, and loam, a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay, is usually best for farming.

Wind and rain can carry soil away, especially when no plants cover the ground, and this loss is called erosion. Farmers protect soil by growing crops that cover the ground and by adding compost, a mixture of decayed food scraps and leaves. In Saudi Arabia, where many soils are sandy, a plan to plant ten billion trees will also help to anchor the ground so that it is not blown or washed away.

versions.title: Soil: The Living Ground
versions.text:
When you pick up a scoop of soil, it may resemble ordinary dirt, yet soil is one of the most valuable materials on Earth, because almost all of the food that humanity consumes depends upon it, directly or indirectly.

Soil is a mixture of several ingredients. Approximately half of it consists of minerals, which are microscopic fragments of disintegrated rock, while a small proportion is humus, the dark, spongy material that forms when dead plants and animals decay, and the remainder is air and water, which occupy the spaces between the particles.

Soil originates from rock through a process called weathering, in which heat, cold, rain, wind, and ice fracture rock into progressively smaller fragments over many years, while plant roots penetrate crevices and gradually split the rock apart. Because this process is extraordinarily slow, it can take as long as a thousand years to form a single centimeter of soil.

Healthy soil is teeming with life, since a handful can contain more living organisms than there are people on Earth, although the overwhelming majority of them are microscopic. Earthworms excavate tunnels that allow air and water to reach plant roots, and their waste enriches the ground, while decomposers such as bacteria and fungi decompose fallen leaves, and in the process they release nutrients that vegetation requires for healthy growth.

Soil is arranged in distinct horizons, or layers: the topsoil is dark and rich in humus, and it is where most roots develop, while beneath it lies the subsoil, which is paler and contains less humus, and deeper still is solid rock.

Soils also differ considerably in texture. Sandy soil has relatively large grains, so water drains through it rapidly, whereas clay soil has extremely small particles that retain moisture and become sticky, and loam, a balanced combination of sand, silt, and clay, is generally considered ideal for agriculture.

Wind and rain can carry soil away, particularly when no vegetation protects the ground, and this loss is called erosion. Farmers conserve soil by cultivating crops that cover the ground and by incorporating compost, a mixture of decayed food scraps and leaves, and in Saudi Arabia, where many soils are sandy, an ambitious initiative to plant ten billion trees will also help to anchor the ground so that it is not blown or washed away.

keyWords.definition: the hard, solid stuff that mountains and stones are made of

keyWords.definition: the dark, soft part of soil made from dead plants and animals
keyWords.example: The gardener mixed humus into the ground to help her roses grow.

keyWords.definition: a long, thin animal with no legs that lives in the ground
keyWords.example: After the rain, an earthworm wiggled across the path.

keyWords.definition: one level of something that lies on top of or under another
keyWords.example: The cake had a layer of cream in the middle.

keyWords.definition: when wind or water slowly carries soil or rock away
keyWords.example: Erosion made the bank of the stream wash away.

questions.stem: What is the article mostly about?
options: How to dig a hole in a garden
What soil is, how it forms, and why it matters
Why earthworms come up out of the ground after rain
How to plant a tree
questions.why: The article tells what soil is made of, how it comes from rock, what lives in it, and why we need to protect it.

wrong.A: The article does not teach how to dig.
wrong.C: Earthworms are one part of the article, and it does not explain why they come out after rain.
wrong.D: Trees are mentioned at the end, but the article does not explain how to plant one.

questions.stem: What is humus?
options: A kind of hard rock
A tunnel made by a worm
Dark, soft soil from dead plants
Water that is deep under the ground
questions.why: The article says dead plants rot and turn dark and soft, and this dark part is humus.

wrong.A: Rock is a different part of soil.
wrong.B: Worms make tunnels, but those are not humus.
wrong.D: The article does not call water humus.

questions.stem: How long can it take to make a thin layer of soil?
options: A thousand years
Only about one week
Ten days
One year
questions.why: The article says it can take a thousand years to make a thin layer of soil.

wrong.B: One week is much too short.
wrong.C: Ten days is much too short.
wrong.D: One year is much too short.

questions.stem: The article says the top layer of soil is "rich." What does rich mean here?
options: Full of money and gold
Very wet
Very hard
Full of what plants need
questions.why: The top layer is dark with humus, and most roots grow there, so rich means it has a lot of what plants need.

wrong.A: Soil does not have money; that is a different meaning of rich.
wrong.B: The article does not say the top layer is wet.
wrong.C: The hard part is the rock at the bottom.

questions.stem: What happens when an earthworm digs in the soil?
options: The soil slowly turns back into rock.
Air and water get into the soil.
The soil blows away.
Plants stop growing.
questions.why: The article says air and water go down the paths or tunnels that earthworms make.

wrong.A: Rock turns into soil, not the other way around.
wrong.C: Wind and rain cause erosion, not worms.
wrong.D: Worms help plants; they do not stop them from growing.

questions.stem: Why would a farmer be glad to find lots of earthworms and bugs in a field?
options: They help make the soil good for plants.
They eat up all of the weeds in the field.
They keep the rain away.
They turn the soil into sand.
questions.why: Worms let air and water in, and bugs and germs turn dead leaves into food for plants.

wrong.B: The article does not say worms or bugs eat weeds.
wrong.C: The article does not say worms keep rain away.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article says worms make sand.

questions.stem: A hill has no plants on it. What will most likely happen after a big storm?
options: New soil will form in one night.
The soil will turn into humus.
Some of the soil may wash away.
The hill will grow taller.
questions.why: The article says wind and rain can carry soil away and that roots hold soil in place. With no roots, rain can wash soil off.

wrong.A: Soil forms very slowly, over a very long time.
wrong.B: Humus comes from dead plants, and a storm does not make it.
wrong.D: Erosion takes soil away; it does not make a hill taller.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about Saudi Arabia's plan to plant trees?

To show one way people protect soil
To explain how to cut down trees
To list the fruits that trees give
questions.why: The article says roots hold soil in place, so planting trees is a way to stop erosion.

wrong.A: The article does not compare trees and grass.
wrong.C: The plan is about planting trees, not cutting them down.

options: They turn rock into minerals.
They remove all of the humus from the topsoil layer.
Tunnels let in air and water, and waste enriches it.
They make the soil sticky like clay.
questions.why: The article says earthworm tunnels let air and water reach roots and their waste enriches the ground.

wrong.A: Weathering, not worms, breaks rock down.
wrong.B: Worms add richness; they do not remove humus.
wrong.D: Stickiness comes from clay's tiny particles.

questions.stem: Sandy and clay soils "differ in texture." Which detail best shows what texture means here?
options: Sand drains quickly, but clay is sticky.
Topsoil is darker than subsoil.
Soil can take a thousand years to form.
Saudi Arabia plans to plant ten billion trees.
questions.why: Texture describes how soil feels and how its particles behave, such as large sand grains or sticky clay.

wrong.B: This is about color and layers, not texture.
wrong.C: This is about how long soil takes to form.

questions.stem: Why does water drain quickly through sandy soil?
options: Sandy soil contains more humus.
Sandy soil is always frozen.
Sandy soil has no minerals.
Sandy soil has large grains.
questions.why: The article explains that sandy soil has large grains, so water drains through it quickly.

wrong.A: The article does not say sandy soil has more humus.
wrong.B: Nothing in the article says sand is frozen.
wrong.C: Sand grains are themselves bits of mineral.

questions.stem: Why does the author state that a centimeter of soil can take a thousand years to form?
options: To show that soil is easy for people to replace
To compare soil with ice
To stress that lost soil is slow to replace
To explain how roots split rock
questions.why: This fact helps readers understand why protecting soil from erosion matters so much.

wrong.A: The fact shows the opposite: soil is very hard to replace.
wrong.B: Soil is not compared with ice.
wrong.D: The time frame does not explain how roots split rock.

questions.stem: Why might a farmer with sandy soil in Saudi Arabia add compost to the fields?
options: Compost turns sand into solid rock.
Compost adds decayed material that enriches soil.
Compost stops the strong sun from heating the ground.
Compost removes all organisms from the soil.
questions.why: Sandy soil drains fast, and compost adds decayed plant material like humus, which enriches soil.

wrong.C: The article does not say compost blocks the sun.
wrong.D: Decayed material feeds soil organisms; it does not remove them.

questions.stem: A forest is cleared to build a road, and heavy rain follows. What is the most likely result?
options: New topsoil will form within a year or two.
The subsoil will turn into humus.
Weathering will stop completely.
Erosion will carry away the soil.
questions.why: The article says erosion is worst when no vegetation covers the ground; without roots, rain can wash soil away.

wrong.B: Rain does not turn subsoil into humus.
wrong.C: Clearing a forest does not stop weathering.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say soil is just dirt and does not need protecting. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
